definition: Gluttony means overindulgence in food or drink.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word gluttony. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know gluttony should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After a week of holiday gluttony, even the dog turned down table scraps.
Appetite is the body's honest wanting, and it switches off when fed; gluttony is what keeps eating after the switch.
An indulgence is one knowing step past need — dessert on a Tuesday; gluttony makes excess the whole meal, and the meal after that.

Overindulgence is too much of any pleasure — screens, spending, sleep, sweets. Gluttony is overindulgence kept to the table: eating and drinking carried on past fullness. Every bout of gluttony is overindulgence, but only the food-and-drink kind earns the older, harsher word.

Greediness is grasping for more of anything — money, food, praise — and hoarding it whether or not it can ever be used. Gluttony is narrower and bodily: the excess is eaten and drunk on the spot. The greedy keep what they gain; the glutton swallows it.

Thanksgiving at Uncle Ray's follows a script: a third plate after the second, a fourth wedge of pie 'to even out the pan,' the belt loosened one hole at a time, and then the long groan from the couch.
Nobody at that table is hungry past two o'clock.
What happens after two is gluttony.
Gluttony is the right word because appetite has an end and this eating doesn't respect it.
Appetite is the body's honest wanting; gluttony begins where want ends and the indulging keeps going — plates after fullness, driven by the pleasure of excess itself.
Gluttony carries the weight of the old list of deadly sins — it judges, and it stays at the table: food and drink.
Insatiable, its unit-mate, names a different condition: hunger (for anything — praise, facts, profit) that no amount ever satisfies.
The glutton overshoots fullness; the insatiable never reach it.

Roman satirists loved to skewer the banquets of the newly rich.
In one famous scene, a host serves twelve courses to guests who stopped being hungry at the second, and peacocks arrive dressed in their own feathers.
The poet's target was not wealth itself but gluttony — the eating that keeps on long after hunger has left the room.
Guests, he notes acidly, reached for delicacies while still describing the last ones as too much.
Hunger, the satire insists, is innocent; what happens at the tenth course is a choice.
